one_line: Vendor talk (DZ Labs, now Colibra) on turning millions of messy SharePoint documents into AI-ready data by tagging, deduplicating, freshness-filtering and scoping them before RAG.
summary: Jeff Koss and Leo Platzer, from DZ Labs (acquired by Colibra), walk through a fictional manufacturer that wants a legal-ops chatbot over SharePoint. Their pilot used 40 pre-curated files and worked, but at 80,000+ files the team could not find relevant files, could not find sensitive data, and could not trust the quality. The talk's pitch is that a repeatable pipeline for unstructured data (classify, scan, dedupe, freshness-filter, slice, refresh) is what moves a stalled POC into production. The demo covers an AI-suggested tag tree with conditional sub-tags and per-tag evidence, a hybrid pattern-plus-AI sensitivity scan, a dedup/freshness dashboard, and "data slices" that auto-refresh on a schedule. Leo argues that stale and duplicate chunks crowd out relevant results in top-K retrieval, and cites an internal multi-hop RAG eval with large recall and task-completion gains. The closing demo generates a context.md index per SharePoint folder so coding agents can read a summary instead of opening files. Most of the talk is product demo; the reusable ideas are the pipeline stages and the claim that corpus hygiene matters regardless of use case, but the numbers are vendor-run and not detailed.

key_ideas.idea: A POC on 40 curated files hides problems that appear at 80,000+ files: discovery, sensitive-data location, and data trust.
key_ideas.detail: The North River example went from a working 40-file pilot to failures in finding relevant files, leaking sensitive data into the chatbot, and wrong answers. The speaker frames the gap between POC and production as a data-curation problem, not a model problem.

key_ideas.idea: Document quality is not tabular quality. Duplication, conflicting versions and freshness matter as much as completeness and accuracy.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker lists the six classic data-quality dimensions and then says documents need checks for duplicate and conflicting content and for how current each file is.

key_ideas.idea: Tag the corpus with an AI-suggested taxonomy that a human reviews, then use the tags as chatbot metadata.
key_ideas.detail: A tag tree can have conditional branches (for example, only legal files get a contract-type sub-tag). AI proposes tags from a prompt and optional classification values, a reviewer accepts or rejects them, and thumbs up/down acts as few-shot feedback. Each tag shows the evidence text and a confidence score.

key_ideas.idea: Use a hybrid of pattern matching and AI for sensitive-data detection, with context words to cut false positives.
key_ideas.detail: For a Finnish national ID example, the tool generated a regex and also added Finnish context words that tend to appear near the identifier. The speaker says this reduces false positives compared with pattern-only scanning.

key_ideas.idea: Deduplicate and filter stale files before they reach the index, because redundant context crowds out relevant chunks in top-K retrieval.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker's argument: in a RAG index, duplicate or outdated versions fill the top-K results, so the answer is starved of relevant material. Duplicates are either genuine newer context or pure redundancy and are handled differently.

key_ideas.idea: A corpus with 30% stale or duplicate files can fill up to 80% of an agent's context with stale information, according to the speaker's internal eval.
key_ideas.detail: The claim is from the vendor's own multi-hop RAG evaluation, not a public benchmark. The speaker reports that recall@1 roughly doubled and task-completion accuracy rose 10-15% after cleanup. The talk gives no eval setup, dataset size or baseline details, so the figures are unverified.

key_ideas.idea: Generate a context.md index for each folder so coding agents read a summary before opening files.
key_ideas.detail: The demo fetches SharePoint metadata and writes, for each folder, the document types, key topics, when to use it, and example questions, plus a top-level index. The agent consults the index first and skips folders that are not relevant.

key_ideas.idea: Keep the curated set fresh with scheduled refreshes of a saved slice, so new or deleted source files flow into the index automatically.
key_ideas.detail: A data slice is a saved filter over the metadata (for example, only legal files newer than a date, or at least N required fields). A workflow reruns it on a schedule and the SDK pushes updated metadata into the vector database.

techniques.name: Conditional tag tree with AI suggestions and human review
techniques.how: Define a tag with an LLM prompt and optional allowed values. Let the model propose sub-tags, add branches that only apply when a parent tag matches, and let a reviewer accept or reject each suggestion. Use thumbs up/down as few-shot examples. Store the evidence span and confidence score with each tag.
techniques.when: Classifying a large, mixed document corpus before it goes into RAG, when you need auditable tags and metadata-filtered retrieval.

techniques.name: Dedupe and freshness pruning before indexing
techniques.how: Group duplicate and near-duplicate documents, decide whether each version is newer context or plain redundancy, and drop stale files outside a date window. Apply this step before chunking and embedding.
techniques.when: Document corpora with many versions of the same contract or policy, where old versions would otherwise appear in top-K results.

techniques.name: Hybrid pattern plus LLM sensitive-data scan
techniques.how: Use an LLM to draft a regex for a national ID or similar identifier, then add nearby context words, and run the regex with AI validation on top. Review matches at file and chunk level.
techniques.when: Finding PII or PHI in documents in languages or formats where you cannot write rules yourself.

techniques.name: Folder-level context index file
techniques.how: Write a context.md per folder with document types, topics, when to read it and example questions, plus a root index. Point the coding agent at the index so it reads the summary before opening raw files.
techniques.when: Agents that search large file trees and waste tokens opening irrelevant files.

techniques.name: Scheduled data slices
techniques.how: Save a filter over metadata as a named slice and rerun it on a fixed schedule. The downstream chatbot or vector store then reloads the slice so it stays current.
techniques.when: Enterprise corpora that change continuously, where a stale index would give wrong answers.

tools: DZ Labs (DZ data curation platform, DZ SDK)

numbers.claim: Pilot used about 40 pre-curated files; production target is 80,000+ SharePoint files, and a telecom customer has 20,000 HTML files.
Demo ingested 339 files; filters narrowed the set to about 20, and a legal-only data slice had 14 files.
Speaker's example: 30% of files stale or duplicate can lead to up to 80% of agent context being stale information.
Internal multi-hop RAG eval: recall@1 roughly doubled and task-completion accuracy improved 10-15%. Vendor-reported, no setup given.
Customer case: data preparation fell from about four months to a few days.
Demo fixture: 68 files tagged as contracts and legal; the demo says 40,000 employees across 20 countries (fictional customer).

hot_takes: Stale and duplicate documents can make up most of an agent's retrieved context, so corpus cleanup matters more than retrieval tuning.
Data quality for documents means duplication, conflicts and freshness, not the classic tabular dimensions.
Use case does not change the value of deduplication and freshness, so they are a universal first step.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh ingests knowledge buckets for hybrid BM25+pgvector retrieval, and the talk's dedupe and freshness pruning is a possible ingest step that AgentOS does not do yet. The speaker's eval numbers are unverified.
relevance.action: Build a small multi-hop RAG test set with duplicate and stale versions, then measure recall@1 with and without a dedupe-plus-date-window pruning step in MemoryMesh ingest.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI for long runs. A folder-level context index written before a run could cut the file-scanning tokens the CLI spends, and the auto-refresh idea fits its schedules.
relevance.action: Try writing a context.md index per repo folder before a ProsHarness run and compare the number of file reads the CLI makes on a fixed task with and without it.
